card.text: Silas Crane says he has **bought** the Great Library. His deed is in the Registry, signed by the Keeper herself. Professor Penhallow says she never signed it. At five o'clock today she must hand him the keys, and the doors will close. Read every date. Read every tense. Then read the small print.

cutscene.picture: Frost on the round window; the harbour steams in the cold. Cinnamon buns rise up the dumbwaiter, warm and sticky. Under one bun: a postcard with a puffin stamp. Dev grabs it. Asha grabs Dev.

lines.text: Mum's last one! She says she's coming home.
Read the date first. You always skip the date.

cutscene.picture: Tam's voice, out of breath. Quill is already reaching for the deerstalker.

lines.text: Forum. Now. Mr Crane's put up a notice and the Keeper's gone the colour of milk.
Fewer questions. More bicycles.

cutscene.picture: Gulls wheel and complain overhead. A crowd round the notice board, breath smoking. Crane on the top step, camel coat, red pencil behind his ear, smiling down. Professor Penhallow at the bottom, keys clenched in one fist.

lines.text: I never signed it.
My dear Keeper. The Registry says you did. Five o'clock, on these steps. Do bring the keys.

cutscene.place: Close on the Library's great doors behind them
cutscene.picture: the carved motto lit by the low sun. Above them, the Clock Tower's hands stand at a quarter past eleven. Nell looks up at the motto, just for a second.

lines.text: Every word, for everyone. Not for sale.

cutscene.place: The Comet at the foot of the steps.

lines.text: Hunch-o-meter: this is a forgery, ten out of ten.
Then prove it. With nine of them, at least. You have until five.

cast.name: Silas Crane
cast.look: Tall, silver-templed, a camel coat, a red pencil behind one ear
cast.manner: Smooth and smiling; calls everyone "my friend"; never answers the question asked
cast.motive: he wants the Library for "The Inkwell Experience"
cast.opportunity: the visitor form he carried away on 26 February
cast.secret: the last book he borrowed as a boy, the week his family moved away, is still on his desk, thirty-one years overdue

cast.name: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
cast.look: Short and round, a brown suit one size too big, round spectacles he polishes when anxious, a satchel of papers held like a shield
cast.manner: Anxious and polite; talks in the passive voice when frightened; apologises to furniture
cast.motive: nine years of never saying no to Crane
cast.opportunity: his name is on the witness line
cast.secret: the satchel he will not let go of holds the draft deed in Crane's red pencil, which he has carried everywhere for two weeks "by accident"

cast.name: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
cast.look: Grey bun, Library keys on a ribbon, a pencil in the bun
cast.manner: Crisp, fair, quietly terrified; dates everything
cast.motive: the Scriptorium roof leaks, and the menders want ninety thousand crowns she does not have
cast.opportunity: she did sign a page for Crane
cast.secret: she signed that page folded, without reading it, and has told nobody but her day book

cast.name: Mr Rupert Swale
cast.look: Thin, a coat a size too large since spring, hands red and rough
cast.manner: Stiff and ashamed after the business of the map (Case 8); answers in full sentences

cast.means: six years as her deputy, so he knows her signature better than his own
cast.opportunity: at the Registry the morning the deed was lodged
cast.secret: since February he has been washing pots in his sister's café on the mainland, and is too ashamed to say so

docs.title: Crane's notice: A New Chapter for Inkwell
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: the Forum notice board
docs.picture: a cream poster with a gold border on a cork board, a crowd's shadows across it.
docs.body:
**A NEW CHAPTER FOR INKWELL**

Friends and neighbours, I am delighted to share wonderful news. [[c:annDate|On the fourth of March]], in a quiet office
and before a trusted witness, Professor Orla Penhallow signed the Great Library over to me. [[c:gladly|She did so gladly,
I am sure]], because she knows that a tired old building needs a firm hand.

Nothing will be lost. Everything will be improved. From June, the Library will reopen as The Inkwell Experience, with
guided tours, a gift shop and a café. [[c:tickets|Tickets will be fairly priced.]]

The deed was lodged at the Forum Registry this morning, so everything is entirely proper.
[[c:fiveKeys|At five o'clock today, on these steps, the Keeper will hand me the keys, and the doors will close for
improvements.]]

Questions are welcome at my office on Lamplit Row, although I cannot imagine there will be many.

Change can feel strange. Progress always does.

With warm regards to every reader,
Silas Crane · [[c:noticeDate|03/14]]

docs.title: The deed: a Registry copy
docs.author: typed for Silas Crane; copy certified by Mr R. Osei
docs.where: the Forum Registry, handed over by Mr Osei
docs.picture: a long parchment-coloured sheet with a red wax seal, a neat white gap in one line.
docs.body:
**DEED OF SALE**

[[c:deedDate|This deed is made on 03/04]], at Inkwell.

The Keeper of the Great Library, Professor O. Penhallow, sells the Great Library, with its books, rooms and land, to
Mr Silas Crane.

The Library is sold [[c:gap|in exchange ___ the sum of one hundred thousand crowns]], paid in full.

From the date above, the Library belongs to Mr Crane. He may open it, close it or charge for it as he sees fit.

Signed: *O. Penhallow*, Keeper

[[c:witness|Witnessed by: S. Pettigrew]]

*Clerk's copy note:* there is a neat gap after the word "exchange", the width of one short word.
[[c:gapnote|It was there when Mr Crane opened his own envelope at my desk.]] A small card fell out with the deed.
— R. Osei, Registry clerk

docs.title: The calling card
docs.author: unknown ("B.")
docs.where: inside Crane's envelope, with the deed
docs.picture: a small cream card with one perfect round ink blot in the corner.
docs.body:
A word for a word.
[[c:onlyone|After this, only one is left.]]
[[c:forthwith10|Read on, forthwith.]]
— B.

docs.title: Postcard from Reykjavík
docs.author: Dr Leela Raman
docs.where: the agency's dumbwaiter, under a cinnamon bun
docs.picture: front, a row of painted wooden houses, red, yellow and blue, below a snowy mountain; back, a puffin stamp.
docs.body:
Reykjavík, 4 March

My darlings,

Snow, puffins and a hot spring that smells of eggs! [[c:twoways|Here they write today's date as 4.3, day first, just
like we do at home.]]

I spent the week in an old shipping office, reading Mr Crane's company papers. He bought a little museum here once and
shut it within the year. The people here still miss it.

One thing jumped out. [[c:monthfirst|Every letter Mr Crane ever signed puts the month first, so 03/04 means the fourth of
March to him.]] He has done it for thirty years. Habits are like footprints.

Puzzle for Dev: write the day I posted this card the Inkwell way and the Crane way. Are they the same day?

Asha: check Dev's answer against my date. He forgets which way round.

Home soon. Feed the periscope.

All my love, Mum (Dr L. Raman)

docs.title: Forum Registry day book
docs.author: Mr R. Osei, Registry clerk
docs.where: the Registry counter, open at the day's page
docs.picture: a ruled ledger with a brass corner, a pen in the gutter.
docs.body:
**FORUM REGISTRY — DAY BOOK**

Saturday 14 March

[[c:dayfirst|Registry Rule 1: every date in an Inkwell deed is read day first, then month.]]

8.50 · Visitor in the waiting room: [[c:delia10|Miss Delia Nove, puzzle-setter]], with a newspaper and a violin case.
She asked for nothing. She helped Mr Crane pick up his gloves when he dropped them, and held his envelope.

[[c:lodged|9.05 · Deed of sale lodged by Mr S. Crane, in person.]] A gap found in the wording, and a card. Mr Crane
said, "A printing fault. Lodge it anyway." Lodged.

[[c:queried|9.10 · Date on deed: 03/04. Query sent to Mr Crane's office.]] No reply.

9.40 · [[c:swalepapers|Mr R. Swale called to collect his own papers: a land map he lodged last year.]] He did not ask
about any deed.

11.00 · Mr Crane's notice pinned on the Forum board.

— R. Osei

docs.title: Crane's letter to his partners
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.when: dated 3 March; the envelope is postmarked "Inkwell, 3 March"
docs.where: the *Inkwell Herald* letters desk. A copy was sent to the editor with a note: "Print when I say."
docs.picture: thick grey writing paper, a crane printed in the corner.
docs.body:
**Crane & Partners · Lamplit Row**

[[c:letterDate|3 March]]

Dear Partners,

I write with the news we have waited two years for. [[c:wasSold|The Great Library was sold to me this week]], quietly
and properly, and the paperwork is in my safe.

Our builders can begin in May. The reading rooms will become a café, and the Seal Room will make a charming gift shop.

I expect a little noise from the Keeper, and from the children who run about town with notebooks. Ignore it. Noise is not
a lawyer.

I shall lodge the deed when the moment is right, and announce it the same morning. Kindly keep this letter private until
then.

Yours, with ambition,
S. Crane

P.S. Pettigrew will witness. [[c:psWitness|He is nervous, but he will sign what he is given.]]

docs.title: Mr Pettigrew's statement
docs.author: Mr S. Pettigrew, taken down by Constable B. Tully
docs.where: Constable Tully's notebook, with a cocoa ring on the cover
docs.picture: a constable's notebook, ruled, a pencil stub tied to it with string.
docs.body:
**Statement of Mr Septimus Pettigrew, assistant and lawyer to Mr Crane**

[[c:wasAsked|I was asked to witness the deed]] on the evening of 12 March. The papers were placed on the desk in front
of me. The Keeper's name had been signed already, and the ink was quite dry.

[[c:didNotSee|I did not see it signed.]] I was told that it had been signed properly, earlier. I signed my own name
where a finger was pointing. The lamp was turned down afterwards, and the office was locked.

I should like to say that nothing improper was done. [[c:notIntended|I am sure it was not intended to be.]]

I am sorry to have taken up the Constable's afternoon. I have had very little sleep this week.

Signed, S. Pettigrew

docs.title: Dr Quarrender's report
docs.author: Dr Hollis Quarrender, "Expert in Hands"
docs.where: pinned to the Registry copy of the deed by Mr Crane
docs.picture: heavy paper with a curly letterhead, an eyepiece drawn in the margin.
docs.body:
**Report on a signature, prepared for Mr S. Crane**

I have studied the Keeper's signature on the deed with the greatest care. [[c:beautiful|It is a beautiful, convincing
hand]], confident and graceful. In my long experience, a forger's hand trembles, and this one does not tremble at all.

[[c:feelCertain|I feel certain it is genuine]], and I would be astonished to be proved wrong.

[[c:photo|I examined a photograph of the signature, sent to me by Mr Crane.]] I compared it with the Keeper's signature
on a Library visitor form, also sent to me by Mr Crane. [[c:sameStroke|The two match exactly, stroke for stroke, with
not a hair's difference.]]

Nothing could be more reassuring.

My fee has been paid, with thanks.

Dr H. Quarrender

docs.title: The Keeper's day book and note
docs.author: Professor O. Penhallow
docs.where: the Keeper's desk, the Library day book
docs.picture: a green leather day book, the Keeper's keys on its ribbon lying across it.
docs.body:
**GREAT LIBRARY — KEEPER'S DAY BOOK**

26/2 · Mr Crane visited and asked to see the Seal Room. Refused. [[c:visitorForm|I signed his visitor form at the foot
of a long page; the top was folded over.]] Careless of me. — O.P.

[[c:away|4/3 · Keeper at the Mainland Archives meeting all day. Back 5/3 on the evening ferry.]] M. Finch on the desk.

*Note added 14/3, for the detectives:*

I did not sign any deed. I have asked myself whether that folded page could have been one. It could not.
[[c:carbon|The Library keeps a carbon copy of every visitor form, and mine is in the drawer, top and bottom.]]

[[c:keeperDate|I write every date day first, as you see on every line here.]]

One more thing. [[c:noHand|No one signs their name exactly the same way twice.]] My old teacher, Ada Holloway, taught me
that. If two signatures match perfectly, one of them was copied.

O. Penhallow

docs.title: The Lamplighters' note
docs.author: Tam Bellweather
docs.where: pushed under the agency door
docs.picture: a torn paper bag with flour on it, pencil, no punctuation.
docs.body:
seen mr swale come out of cranes office friday 8 oclock [[c:swaleEnvelope|with a big envelope]] he looked cross not
happy cross like he won something

also [[c:pettBridge|mr p on the bridge after talking to himself i signed i signed i never saw]] he give the ducks his

also a tall lady with a grey plait outside the registry early saturday doing the crossword in ink

docs.title: Mr Swale's letter
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: the Library returns box, among the cookery books; brought by Marlowe Finch, Saturday afternoon
docs.picture: plain paper folded small, a damp ring from a teacup, the corner softened as if it has been held in a wet hand.
docs.body:
Dear Professor Penhallow,

You were right to dismiss me after the business of the map. I have not asked for my post back, and I shall not.

[[c:mainland|Since the twentieth of February I have washed pots in my sister's café on the mainland.]] It is honest work.
I was too ashamed to tell anyone, so I told nobody.

[[c:ferryBack|I came back on Friday's six o'clock ferry, for one reason only.]] Tonight I went to Mr Crane's office for the
last time. [[c:gaveBack|I took a big envelope and gave back every crown he ever paid me.]] He laughed, which made me cross.
Then I walked out, and I felt lighter than I have in years.

[[c:knowNothing|I know nothing about any deed, and I wish to know nothing.]]

Tomorrow I shall collect my own old land map from the Registry, so that none of my papers sit beside his. Then I go back
to my pots.

I could not face your desk, so this goes in the returns box. I am sorry.

Yours, with apology,
Rupert Swale

docs.title: The draft deed
docs.author: typed by S. Pettigrew, corrected in red pencil by S. Crane
docs.where: from Pettigrew's satchel, handed to the child
docs.picture: a typed sheet slashed with red pencil, a coffee ring, a pencilled margin note.
docs.body:
**DRAFT — NOT FOR LODGING**

This deed is made on ______ . *[red: [[c:redDate|03/04. Write it MY way, as always.]]]*

The Library is sold [[c:draftFor|in exchange for the sum of]] one hundred thousand crowns, paid in full. *[red: paid
later. Or not.]*

Signed: ______ , Keeper. *[red: [[c:trace|Trace her name from the visitor form. Slowly.]]]*

Witnessed by: ______ . *[red: [[c:redWitness|P. witnesses. He needn't watch, only sign.]]]*

*Pencil note in the margin, in Pettigrew's hand:* I typed this on 1 March. I did not know then what the red would ask.
I know now, and I am ashamed. — S.P.

docs.title: Silas Crane: "When did the Keeper sign the deed?"
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: Crane's office on Lamplit Row: gaslight burning at noon, a model of "The Inkwell Experience" under glass, the Library's dome with a ticket booth glued to it. A tall clock ticks in the corner. On the desk, under a paperweight, lies a battered children's book with a Library label on its spine.
docs.body:
My friend, it is on the notice and in the deed. [[c:craneFourth|The fourth of March, a perfectly ordinary Wednesday.]]
The Keeper came to my office, she signed, and we shook hands. I offered her a biscuit. She declined, which I thought a
little rude.

docs.title: Silas Crane: "Why did you write to your partners about the sale?"
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: Crane's office on Lamplit Row: gaslight burning at noon, a model of "The Inkwell Experience" under glass, the Library's dome with a ticket booth glued to it. A tall clock ticks in the corner. On the desk, under a paperweight, lies a battered children's book with a Library label on its spine.
docs.body:
[[c:craneAfter|I wrote to them after the sale, naturally.]] One does not tell one's partners about a thing that has not
happened yet. That would be counting chickens. I never count chickens. I buy the farm.

docs.title: Silas Crane: "What does 03/04 mean?"
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: Crane's office on Lamplit Row: gaslight burning at noon, a model of "The Inkwell Experience" under glass, the Library's dome with a ticket booth glued to it. A tall clock ticks in the corner. On the desk, under a paperweight, lies a battered children's book with a Library label on its spine.
docs.body:
It means the date, my friend. The fourth of March. Everybody reads it that way. Well, everybody sensible. I have written
dates the same way all my life, and nobody has ever complained.

docs.title: Silas Crane: "Why do you want the Library?"
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: Crane's office on Lamplit Row: gaslight burning at noon, a model of "The Inkwell Experience" under glass, the Library's dome with a ticket booth glued to it. A tall clock ticks in the corner. On the desk, under a paperweight, lies a battered children's book with a Library label on its spine.
docs.body:
Because free things are forgotten. Nobody values what costs nothing. I used to sit in that Library every afternoon, as a
boy, in the window seat above the harbour. Then we moved away. When I came back, it looked tired. I can make it shine.
Shining costs money.

docs.title: Mr Septimus Pettigrew: "Who asked you to witness the deed?"
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: A bench on the canal bridge. The wind has turned, and smells of rain and river weed. The ducks are watching him hopefully. He has not let go of his satchel once.
docs.body:
I was asked. [[c:pettPassive|The request was made in the office.]] It was made quite firmly. I would rather not say by
whom. Saying it out loud would make it true. I have been trying very hard for it not to be true.

docs.title: Mr Septimus Pettigrew: "When did you sign as witness?"
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: A bench on the canal bridge. The wind has turned, and smells of rain and river weed. The ducks are watching him hopefully. He has not let go of his satchel once.
docs.body: On the evening of the twelfth of March. A Thursday. I remember because Thursday is soup day, and I missed the soup.

docs.title: Mr Septimus Pettigrew: "Did you see the Keeper sign?"
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: A bench on the canal bridge. The wind has turned, and smells of rain and river weed. The ducks are watching him hopefully. He has not let go of his satchel once.
docs.body:
No. I have said so to the Constable. The name was already there. I was told it was all proper. A witness is supposed to
watch, you know. That is the whole meaning of the word. [[c:witnessMeans|To witness is to see a thing done.]] I saw a
thing that was already done.

docs.title: Mr Septimus Pettigrew: "Why did you sign, then?"
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: A bench on the canal bridge. The wind has turned, and smells of rain and river weed. The ducks are watching him hopefully. He has not let go of his satchel once.
docs.body:
Because I have worked for Mr Crane for nine years, and I have always signed. He is not cruel. He simply never hears
the word "no". So I stopped saying it. That was my mistake, not his.

docs.title: Mr Septimus Pettigrew: "Is there anything else we should read?"
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: A bench on the canal bridge. The wind has turned, and smells of rain and river weed. The ducks are watching him hopefully. He has not let go of his satchel once.
docs.body:
*(A long silence. He opens the satchel.)* Yes. I typed the first draft myself, on the first of March. Mr Crane corrected
it in red, as he always does. I kept it. I told myself I kept it by accident. Here. I would like very much to stop being
afraid of a pencil.

docs.title: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper: "Could you have signed the deed by mistake?"
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
docs.where: The Keeper's office: towers of returned books, a cold radiator that knocks like someone asking to come in, the keys on their ribbon. Under the window, a tin bucket catches a slow drip from the ceiling: plink, and a long wait, and plink.
docs.body:
I have asked myself that a hundred times since breakfast. I signed one thing for Mr Crane: his visitor form, on the
twenty-sixth of February. The top was folded. That was careless. But the carbon copy is in my drawer, whole, and it is a
visitor form. I will show you.

docs.title: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper: "Where were you on the fourth of March?"
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
docs.where: The Keeper's office: towers of returned books, a cold radiator that knocks like someone asking to come in, the keys on their ribbon. Under the window, a tin bucket catches a slow drip from the ceiling: plink, and a long wait, and plink.
docs.body:
On the mainland, at the Archives meeting, all day, and very bored. I came back on the evening ferry of the fifth. Marlowe
kept the desk. The ferry ticket is in my coat, if you need it. You probably do.

docs.title: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper: "How do you write a date?"
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
docs.where: The Keeper's office: towers of returned books, a cold radiator that knocks like someone asking to come in, the keys on their ribbon. Under the window, a tin bucket catches a slow drip from the ceiling: plink, and a long wait, and plink.
docs.body:
Day first, then month. Always. It is the Inkwell way, and the Registry's rule. I would sooner write with my left foot
than put the month first.

docs.title: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper: "Why are you so frightened?"
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
docs.where: The Keeper's office: towers of returned books, a cold radiator that knocks like someone asking to come in, the keys on their ribbon. Under the window, a tin bucket catches a slow drip from the ceiling: plink, and a long wait, and plink.
docs.body:
Because the Library's Charter, the one that keeps it free, has been lost for three hundred years. Without it, I cannot
prove the Library may never be sold. I can only prove I did not sell it. Please let that be enough.

docs.title: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper: "Does the Library need money?"
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, the Keeper
docs.where: The Keeper's office: towers of returned books, a cold radiator that knocks like someone asking to come in, the keys on their ribbon. Under the window, a tin bucket catches a slow drip from the ceiling: plink, and a long wait, and plink.
docs.body:
*(She glances at the bucket.)* [[c:roofMoney|Yes. The Scriptorium roof leaks, and the menders want ninety thousand
crowns.]] We have nine. Mr Crane knows it. He offered to "help" in February. I said no, and I would say it again in the
rain.

docs.title: Mr Rupert Swale: "Where were you on Friday at eight o'clock?"
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: The Registry's back bench, in the brown light under the pigeonholes. He holds a rolled land map as if it might bite, and keeps his hands out of sight whenever he can.
docs.body:
At Mr Crane's office, as your Lamplighters saw. I took him a big envelope.
[[c:swaleBusiness|What was in it is between me and Mr Crane.]] He laughed. I left.

docs.title: Mr Rupert Swale: "Tam says you looked cross, like you'd won something."
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: The Registry's back bench, in the brown light under the pigeonholes. He holds a rolled land map as if it might bite, and keeps his hands out of sight whenever he can.
docs.body:
Cross, certainly. He laughed at me. As for my face, I shall not explain it to a paper bag. *(Then, more quietly.)*
Something was won on Friday. Not by him.

docs.title: Mr Rupert Swale: "Why were you at the Registry this morning?"
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: The Registry's back bench, in the brown light under the pigeonholes. He holds a rolled land map as if it might bite, and keeps his hands out of sight whenever he can.
docs.body:
To take my own old land map out of it. I lodged it last year, before all this. I did not want anything of mine in the
same building as anything of his. Mr Osei will tell you I never went near the deed.

docs.title: Mr Rupert Swale: "Who could have written the deed?"
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: The Registry's back bench, in the brown light under the pigeonholes. He holds a rolled land map as if it might bite, and keeps his hands out of sight whenever he can.
docs.body:
Not the Keeper. In six years as her deputy, I never once saw her put the month before the day. She would rather eat a
book. [[c:knowHand|I know her signature better than my own.]] I posted a thousand letters with it. Look for someone who
writes dates the other way round.

docs.title: Mr Rupert Swale: "Where have you been since February?"
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: The Registry's back bench, in the brown light under the pigeonholes. He holds a rolled land map as if it might bite, and keeps his hands out of sight whenever he can.
docs.body:
[[c:notSay|Away. I would rather not say where.]] It is nothing I am proud of. *(He puts his hands in his pockets. Before
he does, you see them: pink and rough, as if they have been in hot water for weeks.)*

docs.title: Dr Hollis Quarrender: "What did you examine?"
docs.author: Dr Hollis Quarrender
docs.where: His study: a velvet chair, magnifying glasses of every size, a stuffed owl with one glass eye that seems to follow you. Dust turns slowly in the window light.
docs.body:
A photograph of the signature, my dear detective, and a very fine photograph it was. Mr Crane was kind enough to post it.
In my long experience, a good photograph tells you everything.

docs.title: Dr Hollis Quarrender: "Did you see the real deed?"
docs.author: Dr Hollis Quarrender
docs.where: His study: a velvet chair, magnifying glasses of every size, a stuffed owl with one glass eye that seems to follow you. Dust turns slowly in the window light.
docs.body:
The real deed? Well. No. It was locked in Mr Crane's safe, and then it was at the Registry, and I was very busy with a
duchess's diary. A photograph is very nearly the same thing. And, between ourselves, my eyes are not what they were. A
photograph can be made very large.

docs.title: Dr Hollis Quarrender: "You say the two signatures match stroke for stroke. Is that good?"
docs.author: Dr Hollis Quarrender
docs.where: His study: a velvet chair, magnifying glasses of every size, a stuffed owl with one glass eye that seems to follow you. Dust turns slowly in the window light.
docs.body:
It is splendid! Identical! Every loop, every curl. [[c:quarrenderIdentical|I have never seen two signatures so
perfectly the same.]] *(A pause.)* Never, in forty years. Not once. Oh dear.

docs.title: Dr Hollis Quarrender: "Who paid you?"
docs.author: Dr Hollis Quarrender
docs.where: His study: a velvet chair, magnifying glasses of every size, a stuffed owl with one glass eye that seems to follow you. Dust turns slowly in the window light.
docs.body:
Mr Crane. Generously. I see now that I was paid to have an opinion, and I gave him a lovely one. I shall write to the
Registry and withdraw it. An opinion is not a fact, however nicely it is dressed.

deductions.label: meaning (date order)
deductions.statement: In Inkwell, the deed's date is a day that hasn't happened yet.
deductions.why: read by Inkwell's rule, 03/04 is the **third of April**. The deed was lodged on 14 March, so it claims to have been signed nearly three weeks in the future. As written, it cannot be valid.
hints: Which way round does Inkwell read a date? There's a rule. It's printed at the top of a page.

deductions.label: voice (whose habit)
deductions.statement: The person who wrote the date puts the month first: Crane, not the Keeper.
deductions.why: the date on the deed is in Crane's habit, not the Keeper's. **Step one of the two-step inference:** if Crane wrote the date, he meant 4 March, which matches his own notice ("On the fourth of March").
hints: Mum's postcard isn't only a puzzle. She says what Crane *always* does. Who else writes dates, in this case, and which way round?

deductions.label: contradiction (tense and date)
deductions.statement: Crane wrote that the Library *was sold* the day before the sale.
deductions.why: **step two.** Taking Crane's own reading (4 March), his letter of 3 March speaks of the sale in the past tense a day before it supposedly happened. The postmark fixes the letter's date. Crane's interview claim ("after the sale") is the one lie he tells. Either reading of 03/04 makes the deed impossible: a future date in Inkwell's order, or a sale described as finished before it began in Crane's.
hints: A man may write a letter before or after a thing. His verb tells you which he thought it was. Read the *verb*, then read the *date*.
deductions.hintNote: by speaking-tube from No. 9, tea going cold

talk.text: He wrote it before it happened! Run to the Registry, before him and Pettigrew leave town!

talk.note: already halfway out of the door, calls back
talk.text: Before *he* and Pettigrew leave. Subject, not object. Now, run!

deductions.talkTrigger: When the child links D3 (the letter and the notice), the string turns gold.

deductions.label: fact-opinion
deductions.statement: The expert's report is opinion dressed as fact; its one real fact shows a tracing.
deductions.why: "beautiful", "convincing" and "I feel certain" are opinions. The facts are that he saw only a photograph, and that the signature is identical to the visitor form. Since no one signs exactly the same way twice, a perfect match proves the signature was copied from the form.
hints: A peacock's tail is very fine, and it tells you nothing about the road.

talk.text: She means the expert's adjectives are pretty and prove nothing. Footnote to the footnote: peacocks can't read.

deductions.label: meaning (the passive voice)
deductions.statement: Pettigrew's statement hides who asked him; the draft names him.
deductions.why: "was asked" never says *who* asked. Crane's own P.S. and red pencil fill the gap. And a witness who "did not see it signed" has not witnessed anything ("To witness is to see a thing done"). The deed's witness line is empty in all but ink.
hints: *I was asked.* By whom? The sentence has a hole in it, exactly the shape of a person. Find a document that fills it.

deductions.label: meaning (the vanished word)
deductions.statement: The gap in Crane's deed is the word FOR, and the Blot took it before we arrived.
deductions.why: "in exchange ___" can only take *for*, and the draft proves it. The gap was there before the deed reached the Registry counter, so the Blot reached Crane's deed first. The Ledger now has ten words, and the card says one is left.
hints: In exchange ___ the sum. Try every short word you know. Only one of them lets you breathe at the end of the sentence.

deductions.label: the unreliable narrator
deductions.statement: Its purpose is to persuade, not to report.
deductions.why: "She did so gladly, I am sure" is an opinion about someone else's feelings. "Everything will be improved" and "Tickets will be fairly priced" are promises, not facts. The only checkable claim in it, the date, is the one that collapses (D1–D3).

deductions.label: the impossible thing
deductions.statement: The Keeper was on the mainland, so her perfect signature was traced from the folded visitor form she signed for Crane on 26 February.
deductions.why: it answers *how could she?* without magic. She could not sign on Lamplit Row from the mainland, and she did not. Her real signature went to Crane's office on 26 February, at the foot of a folded page, and was traced from there, so slowly that it came out too perfect. It does not count toward the accusation, but it is the case's "aha".

redHerrings.title: the Keeper signed it by mistake.
redHerrings.raisedBy: She admits she signed a folded page for Crane, and the Library needs money badly.
redHerrings.note: The folded page was a visitor form, and its carbon proves it. She was not even in Inkwell on 4 March. Crane did use that form, though, as the thing he traced (D4).

redHerrings.title: Swale, back for more (the false solution).
redHerrings.raisedBy: Seen leaving Crane's office with a big envelope "like he won something", then at the Registry on the morning the deed was lodged. He knows the Keeper's hand better than anyone, she dismissed him, and he will not say where he has been.
redHerrings.note: His secret clears him. He was on the mainland from 20 February to Friday 13 March, so he was washing pots when the Keeper signed the visitor form (26/2) and when Pettigrew found her name already signed and dry (12 March). The envelope went *into* Crane's office full of Crane's own money. "Like he won something" was relief. At the Registry he arrived after the deed was lodged and took only his own map. And a forger who knew her hand by heart would not need to trace it.
redHerrings.clearedWhen: DOC 10.11, chapter 4, and the Registry's times

redHerrings.title: Pettigrew, the witness with a satchel.
redHerrings.raisedBy: His name is on the deed, he talks to himself on bridges, he will not open his satchel, and by half past two he has a ticket out of town.
redHerrings.note: He signed a line he should not have, and he knows it. But the satchel holds the draft that names who asked him, and the ticket was bought for him, not by him. Saying no is the one thing he has never practised.

evidenceRule.text: exactly these three: D1, D3 and D4. D2, D5 and D6 are also accepted alongside them: they strengthen the case, but none of them replaces D1, D3 or D4. D1 proves the deed cannot stand as written; D3 proves Crane knew it was a story before it "happened"; D4 proves the Keeper's name was traced, not signed.

wrongSuspect.pettigrew: He signed something he should not have, and he knows it. But read his words again: 'I did not see it signed.' Show me where *he* made the Keeper's name. Who asked him? The sentence won't say. Find a document that will.
wrongSuspect.penhallow: She did sign one folded page, and the roof does leak. Now read what's in her drawer. And where was she on the fourth? A Keeper on the mainland signs nothing in Lamplit Row.
wrongSuspect.swale: Your hunch-o-meter liked him, Nell, and so did mine for a while. Read the letter from the returns box. Where was he on the twenty-sixth of February? Then read the Registry's times. He came *after* the deed.
wrongSuspect.quarrender: He's guilty of something, but it's carelessness, and a little vanity. He gave an opinion about a photograph. Ask who sent the photograph.

accusation.weakEvidence: That's a feeling, and a good one. But a magistrate needs a date she can count on her fingers. Find me the day that hasn't happened yet, or the tense that came too early.

reveal.text: Mr Crane, your deed says it was made on 03/04.
The fourth of March. Shall we move on?
*(the day book)* Registry Rule 1: day first. That's the third of April. Your deed was signed on a day that hasn't happened yet.
*(a little less smiling)* A matter of style.
*(The postcard.)* "Every letter Mr Crane ever signed puts the month first." And it was there from the very first page. *(The notice.)* You dated your own notice 03/14. There is no fourteenth month.

So you meant the fourth. *(The letter.)* Dated the third of March: "The Great Library *was sold* to me this week." Yet you told us, "I wrote to them after the sale, naturally." Footnote: *was sold* is finished. On the third, the sale hadn't started.
*Had not* started. Contractions in court, Felix? Carry on.
And my name? I was on the mainland all that day.
(The child lays the expert's report beside the draft deed. Red pencil: "Trace her name from the visitor form. Slowly.")
*(very small)* Too perfect. Oh dear. I should have worn my spectacles.
You signed one folded page, Professor: his visitor form. He carried it away and traced it. Not Mr Swale: he was washing pots on the mainland, and came home only to give the money back.
*(scarlet, hands behind his back)* Every crown.
(The door bangs. Mr Pettigrew, soaked, holds up a ferry ticket torn in two.)
I was asked to witness. I will say it properly now. *Mr Crane* asked me. I did not see it signed. Nobody saw it signed, because nobody signed it.
(A long silence. Crane takes the red pencil from behind his ear and turns it over.)
It would have been beautiful, you know. The Experience. Gold rope. A little shop. I'd have mended your roof.
I'd rather a bucket than a ticket. It is beautiful *now*. It is beautiful at four o'clock on a wet Tuesday, when a child who has nowhere else to go comes in and is warm.
*(quietly)* I know. I used to be that child.
(He puts the pencil on the table, next to the gavel. Outside, the Clock Tower strikes four. Nobody hands anybody any keys.)
*(arriving, dripping, cocoa in hand)* I was down at the quay. Have I missed it?
By ten minutes. As usual. Sit down; you're just in time for the paperwork.

epilogue.text: The sale is void

Mr Osei writes one line in the Registry day book, in his unhurried hand: *"Deed of 03/04 struck out. Date impossible. Signature traced. Witness saw nothing. — R. Osei."* Then he blots it, which makes Dev jump.

Dr Quarrender's letter of withdrawal arrives by the afternoon post. It is three pages long and contains the phrase "in my long experience" eleven times. On the last page it says, simply, "I was wrong. I am sorry."
No. 9 Lantern Row, that evening
The fire is lit. Semicolon is asleep on the cello's scroll. Ada's tea, as usual, has gone cold beside her.

Silas Crane comes to the door alone, without his coat. Mrs Achterberg lets him in and says, "A cart before the horse goes nowhere, however fine the cart." He does not understand her. Then, standing in the hall, he does.
The detectives are in the kitchen. They are not supposed to be listening. They are listening.
You used to sit in the window seat above the harbour. Third shelf of the sea stories. You read with your mouth moving.
You remember that?
I remember everyone who reads with their mouth moving. They're the ones who mean it.
I wrote the letter on the third because I was certain. I'd planned it so carefully that it felt finished. I wrote *was* because in my head, it already was.
That is the oldest mistake in the world, Silas. Telling a story in the past tense before you've lived it.
Will she prosecute? The Keeper?
That's for the magistrate. But I'll tell you what I'd want, if I were the Keeper. I'd want you inside the building. Not owning it. Shelving it.
(Crane laughs, then stops, because she isn't joking.)
He takes something from his pocket and puts it on the table beside the cold tea: a small, battered book with a Library label on its spine.
*The Lighthouse Boy.* Third shelf of the sea stories. I took it out the week we moved away. It is thirty-one years overdue.
Then take it back yourself, on Monday. Hand it to the Keeper. She'll want to see your face when you do.

When he goes, the fog has come up from the harbour, and the gas lamps of Lantern Row wear it like wool. Mrs Achterberg shuts the door behind him and says, to nobody in particular, "Late fruit is still fruit."
The magistrate's decision
On Monday, Magistrate Ruth Abernethy reads every document twice, which Quill says is the mark of a good magistrate.

"The deed is void," she says. "Mr Crane, you tried to sell what was never yours, using someone else's name. You will volunteer at the Great Library for one year. Two afternoons a week, and Saturday mornings. You will shelve, mend and fetch. You will not be in charge of anything, including the biscuits."
Mr Crane returns *The Lighthouse Boy* to the Keeper before the hearing, and pays the fine out of his own pocket, in small coins, one at a time. It takes some while.

Mr Pettigrew, for his honesty, receives a warning and a handshake. He asks the magistrate whether the Library needs a lawyer who works for free. She says she will pass the question on. He looks as though someone has given him a medal.
The Ledger
That night, the child opens the Blot Ledger and writes the tenth word in ink: **FOR**.
UNDER · THE · CLOCK · THAT · NEVER · STRIKES · LIES · EVERY · WORD · FOR · ______
"It's one word short," says Dev. "And the Blot got to Crane's deed *before* we did. Before anyone did. The Blot is ahead of us."
"The Blot held his envelope," says Asha slowly, looking at the Registry day book. "Eight-fifty. Miss Delia Nove, puzzle-setter. Violin case."
"A tall lady with a grey plait," says Nell, reading Tam's note again. "Doing the crossword in ink."
Asha unfolds the newspaper from the Registry bench. The crossword is finished in ink, every square, except three, in a row, in the very middle. The clue beside them says: *Not against (3).*
Nobody says anything for a moment. Downstairs, the bakery's ovens tick as they cool.
"Footnote," says Felix. "*For* is one of the oldest words in English. It means 'in place of' and 'on behalf of'. Footnote to the footnote: the motto above the Library door has it too."
He doesn't say anything else. But the child looks at the Ledger for a long time.
Nell's application

On the way home, Nell stops The Comet outside the Constabulary. She takes the application form out of her basket. It has been in there so long that it has a cinnamon smell and a bicycle-chain mark across one corner.
"Hunch-o-meter," says Dev, "on whether they say yes."
"No hunch," says Nell. "Evidence. I'll wait for it."
She posts it. Quill, on the handlebars, says nothing at all, which from Quill is the highest praise there is.
Biscuit

Constable Tully finds Biscuit at last, curled up and snoring in the Registry's tray marked **PENDING**, on top of Mr Swale's old land map. "Pending," says Tully, lifting him out. "That's about right for him."
The office object

Crane's **red pencil** goes on the shelf above Quill's desk, between the map-maker's compass and the message bottle. When the child taps it, a small card appears: *"The past tense is a promise that something has finished. Check that it has."*

drill.title: Two Ways to Write a Day
drill.description: Eight dates appear on postcards, each written with numbers: 03/04, 12/01, 05/06, 11/11, 07/02, 01/12, 10/03, 06/05. Above the washing line, a sign says either **INKWELL WAY (day first)** or **CRANE WAY (month first)**. The child pegs each card under its month. Then a second round mixes in sentences: "On 3 March he wrote that it *was sold*. It was sold on 4 March." The child marks which sentence can't be true.
drill.why: the case turns on knowing that a date's meaning depends on its writer's rule, and that a tense makes a claim about time.

items.prompt: On 3 March he wrote that it *was sold*. It was sold on 4 March.
items.answer: On 3 March he wrote that it *was sold*.
options: On 3 March he wrote that it *was sold*.

backgrounds: The Forum steps, morning: pale March sun, long shadows, a crowd in coats around a cork notice board. The Library's great doors in the distance with the carved motto rendered as an *unreadable* band of carving (no lettering; the motto is set live in text when tapped). This is the last time before Case 11 that the door appears; it should be clearly visible and lit.

The Forum Registry: brass counter, pigeonholes, a tall clock with hands, a waiting room bench. A violin case leans at the end of the bench in the "8.50" panel, its owner hidden behind a newspaper. In the chapter 1 hook the bench is empty: a pale square of sun, the folded newspaper, nothing else.

Crane's office, Lamplit Row: gaslight at noon, a glass case holding a model of the Library with a tiny ticket booth, a heavy black safe, a red pencil, a tall ticking clock, and under a paperweight a battered children's book with a Library label on its spine (his secret, in plain view).
The Keeper's office: returned books in towers, a tin bucket under a drip from the ceiling.

The agency in drizzle: the round window streaked, the harbour slate-grey, the cork board with red string to Swale's portrait (chapter 3), then the washing line from the hat stand to the speaking-tube (chapter 4).
No. 9 Lantern Row, evening: fire, cello, teetering books, Semicolon asleep; the kitchen door ajar with five faces in the gap.
The council chamber: tall windows streaming with rain, gas lamps lit early, long table, the mended gavel, one empty chair until the door bangs open.
props: the deed (cream, red wax seal, a clean gap in one line); the draft deed (typed, slashed with red)
the Reykjavík postcard (front: painted houses below a snowy mountain; puffin stamp; no lettering on the front)
the calling card (cream, one perfect blot)
Tam's flour-dusted paper bag; Swale's big envelope; Swale's letter, softened at one corner
the Registry newspaper, its crossword inked in except three empty squares in a row (no readable lettering: the clue is set live in text)
Pettigrew's ferry ticket, torn neatly in two; *The Lighthouse Boy*, a battered children's book (no readable title on the cover)
Crane's red pencil (the office object): a short, much-sharpened red pencil with a crane stamped in gold on the end.
portraits: Crane: must move from amused to *guilty* to *relieved* over the case; the relieved expression in the No. 9 scene should be the first unguarded face he has shown all season.
Pettigrew: nervous throughout, and *relieved* when he hands over the draft. The relieved expression should look younger.
Penhallow, Swale, Quarrender: the full set of six. Swale's hands are pink and rough (pot-washing), and he hides them in most poses.
Miss Delia Nove is *not* portrayed in this case: only a violin case, a grey plait over a shoulder, a newspaper.
art.notes: No lettering in any painting. Documents, notice and deed are set live; the motto on the door is carved texture only.

revealSetting: The council chamber, ten to four. Rain streams down the tall windows. Crane is still smiling, and checking his watch.

aside.text: The clock: at five o'clock today the Keeper must hand Crane the Library's keys on the Forum steps, and the doors close "for improvements"; halfway, Crane moves it to four, and books his only witness onto the four o'clock ferry

The impossible thing: on the fourth of March the Keeper was on the mainland all day, yet her signature is on a deed "signed in a quiet office" on Lamplit Row, so perfect that the expert has never seen two signatures so alike

The false solution: Mr Rupert Swale, the Keeper's old deputy, who knows her hand better than his own, won't say where he has been, and walked out of Crane's office with a big envelope; Nell rates him ten. Broken in chapter 4 by DOC 10.11, his letter from the Library returns box: he has been washing pots on the mainland since before the visitor form was signed
Hidden in plain sight: the date at the foot of Crane's own notice, "03/14". There is no fourteenth month

Saturday 14 March. A cold, bright morning on the Forum steps, with a wind off the harbour that turns the pages of everything. A crowd around the notice board. Professor Penhallow is white to the lips. The Library's great doors, with the motto carved above them, are behind her. Somewhere in the crowd a man is already measuring them with a tape.

aside.where: Chapter 1 — hook (the impossible thing; the Blot is close)
aside.text: The Forum Registry's waiting room. The clock above the counter ticks so loudly that it seems to be counting. A pale square of sun lies across an empty bench.

lines.text: On the bench, folded neatly, is a newspaper. Its crossword is finished in ink, almost every square. The room smells faintly of violets, though there is not a flower in the building.
*(the Keeper's day book in one hand, Dr Quarrender's report in the other)* On the fourth of March she was on the mainland. All day. And her name is on the deed, perfect to the last curl.
So how does a Keeper on the mainland sign a deed on Lamplit Row?
*(sniffing)* And who does a crossword in ink?
Five o'clock, detectives. Questions later. Interviews now.

aside.where: Chapter 2 — hook (escalation: the keys at four, the witness on the four o'clock ferry)
aside.text: The canal bridge, half past two. The sky has gone the grey of old pewter, and the first drizzle freckles the water. Constable Tully arrives at a jog, holding his helmet on.

lines.text: Two bits of news, and neither of them is cocoa. Mr Crane's moved the keys. Four o'clock now, not five. "The light is better for the photographs," he says.
And he's bought Mr Pettigrew a ticket on the four o'clock ferry. A long holiday, he says. Paid.
Mr Pettigrew takes a ferry ticket out of his satchel, as if he had forgotten it was there, and looks at it for a long time. He does not say whether he will go.
The only witness, on a boat, at the exact minute the keys change hands.
Ninety minutes, then. It sounds longer than an hour and a half. Spend it like an hour.

aside.text: Crane's notice (DOC 10.1). Its purpose is to persuade, not to report. "She did so gladly, I am sure" is an opinion about someone else's feelings. "Everything will be improved" and "Tickets will be fairly priced" are promises, not facts. The only checkable claim in it, the date, is the one that collapses (D1–D3).

aside.where: Chapter 3 — The plant (for Case 11; not needed to solve this case)
aside.text: "Miss Delia Nove, puzzle-setter", in the waiting room with a violin case, held Crane's envelope at 8.50. Tam saw "a tall lady with a grey plait". The card ends "Read on, forthwith." The child may pin these; the Board accepts them as "noted for later" and the Ledger shows a small question mark. Not marked, and not explained: the Registry waiting room smells of violets after she has gone, and her newspaper's crossword is finished in ink, almost every square (chapter 1 ends; paid off in the epilogue).

aside.where: Chapter 3 — the board's wrong answer (the false solution)
aside.text: The agency, ten past three. Drizzle on the round window; the harbour has gone the colour of a slate. Downstairs, the bakery's ovens tick. Nell pins Mr Swale's portrait in the middle of the cork board and runs red string to four cards: Tam's "big envelope", the Registry's 9.40, "I know her signature better than my own", and "I would rather not say where".

lines.text: Hunch-o-meter: ten. Look at the draft. Mr Crane told *somebody* to trace her name. Who knows the Keeper's hand better than anyone alive? Her old deputy. She dismissed him. He was Crane's man on the map. He walks out of Crane's office with a big envelope, looking as if he's won. Next morning, he's at the Registry. And he won't say where he's been for three weeks.
*(unclipping a small pair of silver handcuffs he has never once used)* I'd rather not. But it does fit.
Footnote: it fits *beautifully*. Footnote to the footnote: so did Dr Quarrender's report.
Ten again, Nell. And fifty minutes to four.

aside.text: Feet on the thirty-nine stairs, taking them two at a time. Marlowe Finch bursts in, out of breath, holding too many books and one envelope.

lines.text: The Library returns box. It was in with the cookery books. It's for the Keeper, and it's Mr Swale's hand.
Everyone looks at the portrait in the middle of the board. Nobody touches the string.

aside.text: The agency, a quarter past three. Professor Penhallow has come up all thirty-nine stairs without stopping, which she says is nothing after a week like this. She opens the envelope with a paperknife. Everyone reads over her shoulder, which Quill says is rude, and then does too.

aside.where: Chapter 4 — after DOC 10.11 (the false solution breaks)
aside.text: Nell reads it twice. Then she takes out her pencil and crosses out the ten, slowly, so that everyone can see.

lines.text: He went to the mainland on the twentieth of February. The Keeper signed the visitor form on the twenty-sixth. He was washing pots while somebody else had her name.
And the envelope went *in* full. "Like he won something." He had. *(Quietly.)* I gave him a ten. I'm sorry.
*(folding the letter very small)* Pots. Oh, Rupert.
*(putting the handcuffs away, enormously relieved)* Then who did the tracing?
Whoever had the form. Put it on the line, and see who carried it away.

aside.text: Asha pegs the last card. Down at the quay, the ferry gives one long, low hoot: twenty minutes to four. Through the round window, far below on the Forum steps, a camel coat. A man looking at his watch.

lines.text: Mr Pettigrew's on that boat.
Then we are not. Council chamber. Run.

aside.text: The Forum's council chamber, ten to four. Rain on the tall windows; the gas lamps lit early. The mended gavel from Case 4 sits on the table. Four of the five suspects face the child. The fifth chair, Mr Pettigrew's, is empty. Mr Osei has brought the Registry day book. Constable Tully has gone down to the quay.
Silas Crane forged the deed of sale.

exactly these three: D1, D3 and D4. D2, D5 and D6 are also accepted alongside them: they strengthen the case, but none of them replaces D1, D3 or D4. D1 proves the deed cannot stand as written; D3 proves Crane knew it was a story before it "happened"; D4 proves the Keeper's name was traced, not signed.

exercises.prompt: Dr Raman writes: "Here they write today's date as 4.3, day first, just like we do at home." Which month does 4.3 name?
exercises.explain: Day first means the first number is the day and the second is the month. So 4.3 is the fourth day of the third month: 4 March, the date at the top of her card.

exercises.prompt: Tam writes: "seen mr swale come out of cranes office friday 8 oclock". Which word needs an apostrophe to show that the office belongs to Mr Crane?
exercises.explain: The office belongs to Crane, so it is "Crane's office": an apostrophe and s show who owns something. "oclock" needs one too (o'clock), but that apostrophe stands for missing letters, not for an owner.

exercises.prompt: Mr Pettigrew says: "To witness is to see a thing done." What should the witness to a deed have done?
options: Kept it locked away in a safe
exercises.explain: Pettigrew gives you the meaning himself: to witness is to see a thing done. A witness to a signature must watch the signing. Signing afterwards, without seeing it, is not witnessing.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence from Dr Quarrender's report is a fact, something you could check?
options: It is a beautiful, convincing hand
I feel certain it is genuine
My fee has been paid, with thanks.
exercises.answer: My fee has been paid, with thanks.
exercises.explain: You could check whether a fee was paid. "Beautiful", "convincing", "I feel certain" and "reassuring" are his feelings about the signature. They sound grand, but you cannot check a feeling.

exercises.prompt: Mr Pettigrew writes: "I should like to say that nothing improper was done." What does the "im" at the start of "improper" do?
exercises.explain: "Im-" is a prefix meaning "not", like "un-". Improper means not proper: not done the right way. You will also meet it in "impossible" and "impatient".

exercises.prompt: Dr Raman writes about Mr Crane's dates: "He has done it for thirty years. Habits are like footprints." What does she mean?
options: A habit leaves a trail you can follow
Old habits wash away like footprints
exercises.answer: A habit leaves a trail you can follow
exercises.explain: This is a simile: it uses "like" to compare two things. Footprints show where someone has been. A habit, such as always writing the month first, shows on every page a person writes, so a reader can follow it back to them.

exercises.prompt: Tam saw Mr Swale looking "cross like he won something". His letter says: "I took a big envelope and gave back every crown he ever paid me." What had he won?
exercises.explain: Swale won nothing you could hold. Giving the money back let him stop feeling ashamed: he "felt lighter than I have in years". Tam saw the look on his face and guessed at the wrong kind of winning.

exercises.prompt: Crane's letter is dated "3 March" and says: "The Great Library was sold to me this week". His notice says the Keeper signed "On the fourth of March". What is wrong?
options: The letter is written in the future tense
The letter calls the sale finished a day before it
The two papers give the same date
Nothing: the letter came after the sale
exercises.answer: The letter calls the sale finished a day before it
exercises.explain: "Was sold" is the past tense: it tells you the writer thinks the sale has already happened. On 3 March, by Crane's own notice, the signing was still a day away. A past tense is a claim that something has finished. Check that it has.

exercises.prompt: The Registry's rule: "every date in an Inkwell deed is read day first, then month." The deed says "03/04". Read by that rule, which date is it?
exercises.explain: Day first: 03 is the day, 04 is the month, so 3 April. The deed was lodged on 14 March, so by Inkwell's rule it claims a signing nearly three weeks in the future. The same numbers mean 4 March to someone who writes the month first.

exercises.prompt: Crane's notice says of the Keeper: "She did so gladly, I am sure". Why is this an opinion and not a fact?
options: He is guessing at her feelings
It is written in the past tense
exercises.answer: He is guessing at her feelings
exercises.explain: Nobody can see inside another person's head. "I am sure" tells you how Crane feels, not what the Keeper felt. A fact is something you can check; a feeling about someone else's feeling cannot be checked at all.

exercises.prompt: Crane's notice ends: "Change can feel strange. Progress always does." What is the notice mainly trying to do?
options: Persuade readers the change is good
Report what happened, and nothing more
Ask the town for its help
exercises.answer: Persuade readers the change is good
exercises.explain: A notice can report or persuade. This one is full of promises ("Everything will be improved", "Tickets will be fairly priced") and soothing words. It is written to make readers feel the change is fine before they ask questions.

exercises.prompt: Mr Pettigrew says: "The request was made in the office." What does this sentence leave out?
exercises.explain: This is the passive voice: it puts the thing done first and can drop the person who did it. "Someone made the request" would have to name the someone. Frightened people often hide in the passive. Ask: by whom?

exercises.prompt: The deed reads "in exchange ___ the sum of one hundred thousand crowns". Which short word fills the gap?
exercises.explain: You give something "in exchange for" something else. Pettigrew's typed draft has the whole phrase: "in exchange for the sum of". The word that vanished from the deed is FOR.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence best sums up Mr Swale's letter to the Keeper?
options: Swale asks the Keeper to give him back his old post at the Library
Swale has been washing pots, and gave Crane's money back
Swale says he will help Crane to buy the Library
Swale is sending his land map to the Keeper
exercises.answer: Swale has been washing pots, and gave Crane's money back
exercises.explain: A summary keeps the main points. Swale has washed pots on the mainland since February, returned every crown, and knows nothing about any deed. He says he has not asked for his post back, and the map he is collecting, not sending.

exercises.prompt: Dr Quarrender says: "I have never seen two signatures so perfectly the same." Then he says, "Oh dear." Why?
options: He realises a perfect match means one was copied
He thinks the Keeper writes too neatly
He has forgotten to send his bill
exercises.answer: He realises a perfect match means one was copied
exercises.explain: The Keeper's note says: "No one signs their name exactly the same way twice." Real signatures always differ a little. Two that match stroke for stroke mean one was traced from the other, and the expert has just praised a tracing.

exercises.prompt: Tam writes with no punctuation: "mr p on the bridge after talking to himself i signed i signed i never saw". Which version punctuates what Mr P said?
options: Mr P, on the bridge, after talking to himself: "I signed. I signed. I never saw."
Mr P on the bridge "after talking to himself" I signed, I signed, I never saw.
"Mr P on the bridge," after talking to himself, I signed. I signed. I never saw.
exercises.answer: Mr P, on the bridge, after talking to himself: "I signed. I signed. I never saw."
exercises.explain: Speech marks go round the words a person actually said, and only those. Mr P said "I signed. I signed. I never saw." The rest is Tam telling us where and when, so it stays outside the speech marks.

exercises.prompt: Crane signs his notice "03/14". Which number in it must be the month?
exercises.explain: There are only twelve months, so 14 cannot be a month. It must be the day, which means Crane wrote the month first: March the fourteenth, today. It was there from the very first page.

exercises.prompt: Mr Swale hides his hands. They are "pink and rough, as if they have been in hot water for weeks." What has he been doing?
options: Sailing a small boat in winter
exercises.explain: Week after week in hot water leaves hands pink and rough. A clerk's hands would be inky instead. His letter proves it: since February he has washed pots in his sister's café on the mainland.

extraMarks.note: The clock: the keys change hands on the Forum steps at five (moved to four at the end of chapter 2).
